Lecture 1 · M3 Pulse Shaping and ISI · CO3

A square pulse is the worst neighbour on the radio dial

Rectangular pulses are easy to make but their spectrum never ends: the first sidelobe is only 13 dB down and the tails fall slowly. Pulse shaping trades a little complexity for a signal that stays inside its channel.

Relate pulse shape to spectrumState the minimum (Nyquist) bandwidthCompute occupied bandwidth with roll-offExplain adjacent-channel interference
⏱ 40 minBTL-2 Understand · BTL-3 Apply

ConceptTime and frequency are two views of one pulse

A digital signal is a train of pulses \(x(t)=\sum_k a_k\,p(t-kT)\). For random independent symbols its power spectrum is shaped entirely by the pulse:

\[ S_x(f)=\frac{\sigma_a^2}{T}\,|P(f)|^2 \]

Rectangular pulse

\(P(f)=T\,\text{sinc}(fT)\): main lobe to \(\pm R_s\), sidelobes falling as \(1/f^2\) in power. 99 % of the power needs about \(\pm10R_s\).

Shaped pulse

A smooth pulse such as the raised cosine confines the spectrum to \((1+\alpha)R_s/2\) (baseband). Nothing leaks into the next channel.

Analogy: quiet neighboursEach radio channel is a flat in a building. A rectangular pulse is a neighbour who plays music loud enough to be heard three floors away. Pulse shaping is soundproofing: same music, kept inside the walls.

DerivationBandwidth of pulse trains

  1. Spectrum of a random pulse train. With zero-mean, uncorrelated symbols of variance \(\sigma_a^2\), the autocorrelation of \(x(t)\) averages to \(\frac{\sigma_a^2}{T}R_p(\tau)\), so

    \[ S_x(f)=\frac{\sigma_a^2}{T}|P(f)|^2 \]

  2. Rectangular NRZ: \(p(t)=\text{rect}(t/T)\Rightarrow|P(f)|^2=T^2\text{sinc}^2(fT)\). First null at \(R_s\); first sidelobe \(-13.3\) dB; sidelobes decay as \(1/f^2\) (−6 dB per octave in amplitude, the price of a discontinuity).

  3. The smallest possible bandwidth. To send \(R_s\) independent values per second you need at least \(R_s/2\) Hz of baseband bandwidth (Lecture 3 proves this). The ideal pulse is \(\text{sinc}(t/T)\), whose spectrum is a brick wall of width \(R_s/2\).

  4. Practical pulses add an excess bandwidth \(\alpha\) (the roll-off):

    \[ B_{\text{baseband}}=\frac{(1+\alpha)R_s}{2},\qquad B_{\text{passband}}=(1+\alpha)R_s \]

    Practice: every system quotes its roll-off: UMTS 0.22, DVB-S2 0.35/0.25/0.20, many SDR examples 0.35.

  5. Spectral efficiency of M-ary modulation with roll-off \(\alpha\): \(\eta=\log_2M/(1+\alpha)\) bit/s/Hz (passband).

InteractivePulse shape and spectrum side by side

Dots mark the pulse value at other symbol instants t = nT. Grey dots are zero (no ISI); pink dots are non-zero (ISI).

Worked examplesSolved numericals

Example 1 · Nyquist bandwidth minimum
Given: \(R_s=2400\) baud.

\(B_{\min}=R_s/2=1200\) Hz baseband (2400 Hz passband).

Answer: 1.2 kHz baseband.

Example 2 · Raised-cosine bandwidth roll-off
Given: \(R_s=1\) Mbaud, \(\alpha=0.5\).

Baseband \(1.5\times0.5=0.75\) MHz; passband 1.5 MHz.

Answer: 0.75 MHz / 1.5 MHz.

Example 3 · Satellite transponder DVB-S2
Given: 36 MHz transponder, roll-off 0.20.

\(R_s=36/1.2=30\) Mbaud. With 8-PSK: 90 Mb/s before coding.

Answer: 30 Mbaud.

Example 4 · Spectral efficiency QPSK
Given: QPSK, \(\alpha=0.35\).

\(\eta=2/1.35=1.48\) bit/s/Hz.

Answer: 1.48 bit/s/Hz.

Example 5 · Rectangular leakage sidelobes
Given: NRZ at 10 kbaud next to a channel starting 15 kHz away.

At \(1.5R_s\) the sinc² spectrum is about \(-13\) dB below the peak: far too much for a neighbouring channel (typical masks need −40 to −60 dB).

Answer: about −13 dB: pulse shaping is required.

Real worldWhere you meet this

UMTS / 3G

3.84 Mchip/s with root-raised-cosine α = 0.22 fills a 5 MHz channel (3.84 × 1.22 = 4.68 MHz).

DVB-S2 satellite TV

Roll-off 0.35, 0.25 or 0.20 chosen to fit transponder width; DVB-S2X adds 0.15, 0.10, 0.05.

GSM and Bluetooth

Gaussian filtering (BT = 0.3 and 0.5) keeps the spectrum compact for constant-envelope FSK.

Common mistakesWatch out

  • Quoting the first-null bandwidth of NRZ as "the" bandwidth: most of the sidelobe energy lies outside it.
  • Mixing baseband and passband bandwidths: passband is twice baseband.
  • Thinking the sinc pulse is practical: it is infinitely long and very sensitive to timing.

Lecture 2 · M3 Pulse Shaping and ISI · CO3

ISI: when yesterday’s bit is still talking

Send pulses through a channel that is too narrow and each one smears into the next symbol slot. At the sampling instant you read your symbol plus the tails of its neighbours. Too much of that and even a noise-free link makes errors.

Explain how band-limiting causes ISICompute ISI for an RC channelUse peak distortion and worst-case eye openingSeparate ISI from noise
⏱ 45 minBTL-3 Apply · BTL-4 Analyse

ConceptSamples with ISI

The receiver sees \(y(t)=\sum_k a_kh(t-kT)+n(t)\), with \(h\) the overall pulse (transmit filter, channel, receive filter). Sampling at \(t=mT\):

\[ y_m=\underbrace{a_mh_0}_{\text{wanted}}+\underbrace{\sum_{k\ne m}a_kh_{m-k}}_{\text{ISI}}+n_m \]

Peak distortion

\(D=\sum_{k\ne0}|h_k|/|h_0|\). If \(D\ge1\) the eye is closed: some symbol pattern gives an error even with no noise.

Causes

Band-limited cables and filters, multipath echoes in wireless channels, and sampling at the wrong instant.

Analogy: echo in a hallSpeak one word per second in a hall with a two-second echo. Each new word arrives together with the echoes of the last two. Speak slower (lower bit rate) or deaden the hall (wider channel) and the words come through clearly.

DerivationISI of a first-order RC channel

  1. A rectangular pulse of width \(T\) through an RC low-pass with time constant \(\tau=RC\) (bandwidth \(B=1/2\pi\tau\)). Let \(x=e^{-T/\tau}\).

  2. At the end of the pulse (\(t=T\)) the output has risen to the main cursor \(h_0=1-x\).

  3. After the pulse ends, the output decays: at \(t=(n+1)T\) the tail is \(h_n=(1-x)x^n\).

  4. Sum of all tails (geometric series): \(\sum_{n\ge1}(1-x)x^n=x\). The worst pattern (all neighbours opposite) gives the worst-case opening:

    \[ \text{opening}=h_0-\sum_{n\ge1}h_n=1-2x=1-2e^{-T/\tau}=1-2e^{-2\pi B/R_b} \]

  5. Check: \(B=0.25R_b\Rightarrow x=e^{-\pi/2}=0.208\Rightarrow\) opening 0.584; \(B=0.5R_b\Rightarrow0.914\). Program E2 measures exactly these values.

    Design rule: the bandwidth must be a reasonable fraction of the bit rate; below about \(B\approx0.11R_b\) the eye closes completely (\(x\ge\tfrac12\)).

  6. ISI plus noise. With noise std \(\sigma\), the worst-case error probability is \(Q(\text{opening}/\sigma)\) instead of \(Q(1/\sigma)\): ISI acts like a loss of \(-20\log_{10}(\text{opening})\) dB in SNR for the worst patterns.

InteractiveNRZ through a band-limited channel

Top: an 18-bit NRZ sequence (dashed) and the channel output. Dots are samples at the end of each bit: green = correct sign, pink = wrong sign. Bottom: response to a single pulse with the main cursor and the ISI tails.

Worked examplesSolved numericals

Example 1 · RC channel opening
Given: \(\tau=10\ \mu\)s, \(R_b=50\) kb/s (\(T_b=20\ \mu\)s).

\(x=e^{-2}=0.135\); opening \(1-2x\).

Answer: 0.729 (−2.7 dB worst case).

Example 2 · Required bandwidth design
Given: worst-case opening ≥ 0.9.

\(x\le0.05\Rightarrow T/\tau\ge\ln20=3.0\Rightarrow B\ge\frac{3.0}{2\pi}R_b\).

Answer: B ≥ 0.48 Rb.

Example 3 · Peak distortion discrete channel
Given: sampled pulse \([0.2,\ \mathbf{1},\ 0.3]\).

\(D=(0.2+0.3)/1\).

Answer: D = 0.5: eye open, worst opening 0.5.

Example 4 · Maximum bit rate cable
Given: \(\tau=1\ \mu\)s, need opening ≥ 0.8.

\(x\le0.1\Rightarrow T_b\ge\tau\ln10=2.30\ \mu\)s.

Answer: Rb ≤ 434 kb/s.

Example 5 · ISI versus noise error rate
Given: opening 0.584, noise σ = 0.2.

Worst pattern \(Q(0.584/0.2)=Q(2.92)=1.75\times10^{-3}\); without ISI \(Q(5)=2.9\times10^{-7}\).

Answer: ISI raises the worst-case error rate ≈ 6000×.

Real worldWhere you meet this

Telephone-line modems

Early 1200–2400 b/s modems were limited by ISI on 3 kHz phone lines until adaptive equalizers arrived.

Wireless multipath

Echoes from buildings delayed by microseconds smear symbols; at 10 Mbaud a 1 µs echo spans 10 symbols.

USB and PCIe

Gigabit serial links use transmitter pre-emphasis and receiver equalization to undo the cable’s low-pass ISI.

Common mistakesWatch out

  • Blaming errors on noise when the eye is closed by ISI: more transmit power will not help.
  • Sampling at the middle of the bit for a filtered NRZ signal: the best instant is where the eye is widest.
  • Adding the tails with their signs and concluding ISI cancels: the worst case uses absolute values.

Lecture 3 · M3 Pulse Shaping and ISI · CO3

Nyquist’s criterion: the pulse may ring, but it must be silent at the right moments

Zero ISI does not need short pulses. It needs a pulse that is exactly zero at every other sampling instant. Nyquist turned this into a simple test on the spectrum: the shifted copies must add up to a flat line.

State the zero-ISI condition in time and frequencyProve the minimum bandwidth Rs/2Test a spectrum with the folding ruleExplain vestigial symmetry
⏱ 45 minBTL-3 Apply

ConceptThe criterion

Time domain

\(p(nT)=\begin{cases}1&n=0\\0&n\ne0\end{cases}\). The pulse can be long and ring, as long as it crosses zero at every \(nT\).

Frequency domain

\(\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}P\!\left(f-\frac kT\right)=T\) for all \(f\): copies of the spectrum shifted by multiples of \(R_s\) add to a constant.

Analogy: musical chairsEach symbol gets one chair at its sampling instant. Pulses may wander all over the room, but when the music stops (sampling), every other pulse must be standing at zero height.

DerivationFrom zero crossings to a flat folded spectrum

  1. Sample the pulse: \(p_\delta(t)=\sum_np(nT)\delta(t-nT)\). Zero ISI means \(p_\delta(t)=\delta(t)\), whose transform is 1.

  2. Sampling in time makes the spectrum periodic (Poisson sum formula):

    \[ \mathcal F\{p_\delta\}=\frac1T\sum_kP\!\left(f-\frac kT\right) \]

  3. Setting the two equal gives the Nyquist criterion:

    \[ p(nT)=\delta[n]\iff\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}P\!\left(f-\frac kT\right)=T \]

  4. Minimum bandwidth. If \(P(f)=0\) for \(|f|>W\) and \(W<\frac1{2T}\), the copies leave gaps near \(f=\frac1{2T}\) and the sum cannot be constant. So

    \[ W_{\min}=\frac{1}{2T}=\frac{R_s}{2},\qquad p(t)=\text{sinc}(t/T) \]

    Meaning: with bandwidth \(W\) you can send at most \(2W\) independent symbols per second without ISI: the Nyquist rate.

  5. Vestigial symmetry. For \(\frac1{2T}<W<\frac1T\), only adjacent copies overlap. The sum is flat if \(P\) is odd-symmetric about the half-amplitude point \(\frac1{2T}\): \(P(\tfrac1{2T}-f)+P(\tfrac1{2T}+f)=T\). The raised cosine (next lecture) is the standard example.

InteractiveFold the spectrum

Thick: P(f). Dashed: copies shifted by ±Rs and ±2Rs. Pink: their sum. A flat pink line means zero ISI. The triangular spectrum is flat only when its edge is exactly at Rs (slider at 1).

Worked examplesSolved numericals

Example 1 · Ideal Nyquist channel maximum rate
Given: ideal low-pass channel of 4 kHz.

\(R_s=2W=8000\) baud with sinc pulses.

Answer: 8000 baud.

Example 2 · Telephone channel with roll-off
Given: 3 kHz baseband channel, \(\alpha=0.25\).

\(R_s=2W/(1+\alpha)=6000/1.25\).

Answer: 4800 baud.

Example 3 · Triangular spectrum test
Given: \(P(f)=T(1-|f|T)\) for \(|f|\lt 1/T\).

Adjacent shifted triangles add to exactly \(T\) everywhere: Nyquist holds. The pulse is \(\text{sinc}^2(t/T)\), which is zero at all \(nT\ne0\).

Answer: zero ISI (α = 1 case).

Example 4 · Too fast violation
Given: channel bandwidth 0.4 Rs.

\(W\lt R_s/2\): copies leave gaps; no pulse can give zero ISI.

Answer: ISI unavoidable; slow down or widen the channel.

Example 5 · Vestigial check symmetry
Given: \(P(0.5R_s-0.1R_s)=0.8T\).

For zero ISI \(P(0.5R_s+0.1R_s)=T-0.8T=0.2T\).

Answer: 0.2 T.

Real worldWhere you meet this

Every digital radio

RRC transmit and receive filters in LTE, 5G (inside OFDM subcarriers the same idea appears as orthogonality), DVB-S2, satellite modems.

Sampling theorem

Nyquist’s criterion and the sampling theorem are the same mathematics viewed from opposite sides.

Faster-than-Nyquist

Some research systems deliberately send faster than 2W and remove the resulting ISI with heavy processing.

Common mistakesWatch out

  • Thinking zero ISI needs pulses shorter than T.
  • Confusing the Nyquist rate (2W symbols/s) with the Nyquist frequency (half the sample rate).
  • Assuming a Gaussian filter is zero-ISI: it is not; it trades ISI for compactness.

Lecture 4 · M3 Pulse Shaping and ISI · CO3

The raised cosine: the pulse every modem uses

The sinc pulse is perfect on paper and fragile in practice. Add a little excess bandwidth, the roll-off α, and the tails die fast enough that small timing errors no longer matter. Split it into two root-raised-cosine halves and you also get the matched filter for free.

Write the RC pulse in time and frequencyExplain what α tradesExplain RRC transmit/receive filtersDesign an FIR pulse-shaping filter
⏱ 50 minBTL-3 Apply

ConceptThe raised-cosine family

\[ P(f)=\begin{cases}T,&|f|\le\frac{1-\alpha}{2T}\\[2pt]\frac T2\left[1+\cos\!\left(\frac{\pi T}{\alpha}\Big(|f|-\frac{1-\alpha}{2T}\Big)\right)\right],&\frac{1-\alpha}{2T}\lt |f|\le\frac{1+\alpha}{2T}\\[2pt]0,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} \]\[ p(t)=\text{sinc}\!\left(\frac tT\right)\frac{\cos(\pi\alpha t/T)}{1-(2\alpha t/T)^2} \]
Roll-off αBaseband bandwidthTail decayTiming toleranceUsed in
0Rs/21/tnonetheory
0.2–0.250.6–0.63 Rs1/t³smallDVB-S2, UMTS (0.22)
0.350.675 Rs1/t³moderateDVB-S, many SDR examples
1Rs1/t³, fastestlargesteasy timing, wasteful

DerivationWhy it works, and why we split it

  1. Zero ISI. The sinc factor is zero at every \(t=nT\ne0\); the second factor is finite there, so \(p(nT)=\delta[n]\). In frequency, the cosine roll-off is odd-symmetric about \(\frac1{2T}\): vestigial symmetry (L3).

  2. Bandwidth: \(P(f)=0\) beyond \(\frac{1+\alpha}{2T}\), so \(B=\frac{(1+\alpha)R_s}{2}\) (baseband). α is the fraction of excess bandwidth.

  3. Tails. For large \(t\), \(\text{sinc}\sim1/t\) and the second factor \(\sim1/t^2\): the RC tail decays as \(1/t^3\). Sums of tails converge quickly, so a timing error \(\tau\) gives only small ISI \(\sum_{n\ne0}|p(nT+\tau)|\).

  4. Root raised cosine. Put \(\sqrt{P(f)}\) at the transmitter and \(\sqrt{P(f)}\) at the receiver. The cascade is \(P(f)\) (zero ISI), and the receive filter is matched to the transmit pulse (L5), so the SNR is maximal.

    \[ H_{Tx}(f)=H_{Rx}(f)=\sqrt{P_{RC}(f)}\quad\Rightarrow\quad H_{Tx}H_{Rx}=P_{RC},\ \ \text{SNR}=\frac{2E}{N_0} \]

  5. FIR design. Sample \(p(t)\) or \(h_{RRC}(t)\) at \(t=n/\text{sps}\cdot T\) over a span of \(\pm S\) symbols: \(2\,S\,\text{sps}+1\) taps. Typical: sps = 4–8, span 6–10 symbols. Truncation raises sidelobes slightly.

InteractiveRoll-off, tails and timing error

Dots: pulse values at the sampling instants nT + τ. With τ = 0 every pink dot sits on zero for the RC pulse. Move τ and see how quickly ISI grows for small α.

Worked examplesSolved numericals

Example 1 · UMTS channel bandwidth
Given: 3.84 Mchip/s, RRC α = 0.22.

\(B=3.84\times1.22=4.68\) MHz in a 5 MHz channel.

Answer: 4.68 MHz.

Example 2 · Half-way value pulse shape
Given: \(p(T/2)\) for α = 0 and α = 1.

α = 0: \(\text{sinc}(0.5)=2/\pi=0.637\). α = 1: the denominator vanishes; the limit is \(\tfrac\pi4\text{sinc}(0.5)=0.5\).

Answer: 0.637 and 0.5.

Example 3 · Tail size decay
Given: \(t=5.5T\), α = 0 and α = 0.5.

α = 0: \(|\text{sinc}(5.5)|=0.058\). α = 0.5: \(0.058\times|\cos(2.75\pi)|/|1-5.5^2|=0.0014\).

Answer: tail is 40× smaller with α = 0.5.

Example 4 · DVB-S2 carrier transponder fit
Given: 27.5 Mbaud, α = 0.20.

\(B=27.5\times1.2=33\) MHz.

Answer: 33 MHz (fits a 36 MHz transponder).

Example 5 · Filter length FIR design
Given: sps = 8, span ±8 symbols.

\(2\times8\times8+1\).

Answer: 129 taps.

GNU Radio

5G NR

OFDM does not use RC pulses per subcarrier, but windowing and filtering at symbol edges serve the same purpose.

Satellite modems

Common mistakesWatch out

  • Using RC at both ends: the cascade is then RC² which is not Nyquist.
  • Thinking an RRC pulse alone has zero crossings at nT: it does not.
  • Forgetting the special value at t = ±T/(2α) when coding the formula (division by zero).

Lecture 5 · M3 Pulse Shaping and ISI · CO3

The matched filter: the best a linear receiver can ever do

Of all the filters you could put before the sampler, one gives the largest SNR: a filter whose impulse response is the pulse reversed in time. Its peak SNR is \(2E/N_0\), and it is the same thing as a correlator.

Derive the matched filter with Cauchy–SchwarzShow matched filter = correlatorCompute the SNR loss of a mismatched filterConnect RRC filters to matching
⏱ 50 minBTL-3 Apply

ConceptThe problem

Received: \(r(t)=p(t)+w(t)\), with \(w\) white noise of PSD \(N_0/2\). Pass it through \(h(t)\) and sample at \(T_0\). Choose \(h\) to maximise

\[ \text{SNR}=\frac{|y_p(T_0)|^2}{E[n_o^2]}=\frac{\left|\int H(f)P(f)e^{j2\pi fT_0}df\right|^2}{\frac{N_0}{2}\int|H(f)|^2df} \]

Answer

\(h(t)=k\,p^*(T_0-t)\): the pulse, time-reversed and delayed. In frequency, \(H(f)=kP^*(f)e^{-j2\pi fT_0}\).

Maximum SNR

\(\text{SNR}_{\max}=\dfrac{2E}{N_0}\), where \(E=\int|p(t)|^2dt\). Only the pulse energy matters, not its shape.

Analogy: listening for a known tuneIf you know the tune, you hum along and see how well it matches. The matched filter "hums along" with the expected pulse and adds up the agreement over its whole duration.

DerivationCauchy–Schwarz gives the optimum

  1. Cauchy–Schwarz: \(\left|\int A(f)B(f)df\right|^2\le\int|A|^2df\int|B|^2df\), with equality when \(A=kB^*\).

  2. Take \(A=H(f)\) and \(B=P(f)e^{j2\pi fT_0}\). The numerator is bounded by \(\int|H|^2\int|P|^2\), so

    \[ \text{SNR}\le\frac{\int|H|^2df\int|P|^2df}{\frac{N_0}{2}\int|H|^2df}=\frac{2}{N_0}\int|P(f)|^2df=\frac{2E}{N_0} \]

  3. Equality when \(H(f)=kP^*(f)e^{-j2\pi fT_0}\), i.e.

    \[ h_{\text{opt}}(t)=k\,p^*(T_0-t),\qquad \text{SNR}_{\max}=\frac{2E}{N_0} \]

  4. Matched filter = correlator. The output at \(T_0\) is \(\int r(\tau)h(T_0-\tau)d\tau=k\int r(\tau)p^*(\tau)d\tau\): multiply by the expected pulse and integrate. This is exactly the BPSK correlator of Module 2.

  5. Link to BER. For antipodal pulses, \(P_b=Q(\sqrt{\text{SNR}_{\max}})=Q(\sqrt{2E_b/N_0})\): the BPSK formula is the matched-filter result.

  6. Pulse-shaped systems. The transmit pulse is an RRC; the matched filter is the same RRC (it is symmetric). The cascade is RC: zero ISI and maximum SNR at once. This is why every modem uses RRC at both ends.

InteractiveMatched versus mismatched receive filter

A single rectangular pulse in white noise. The readout compares the peak SNR of the chosen filter with the matched-filter bound 2E/N0. The bandwidth slider applies to the RC filter only.

The output is the autocorrelation: a triangle rising to \(A^2T=E\) at \(t=T\), back to zero at \(2T\).

Radar

Pulse-compression radars correlate the echo with the transmitted chirp: a matched filter that also sharpens range resolution.

Common mistakesWatch out

  • Sampling the matched-filter output at the start of the pulse: the peak is at the end (t = T).
  • Thinking a narrower filter always removes more noise: it also removes signal.

Lecture 6 · M3 Pulse Shaping and ISI · CO3

The eye diagram: one picture that tells you if the link works

Overlay the received waveform one symbol period at a time on an oscilloscope and a shape like an eye appears. Its height is your noise margin, its width your timing margin, its slope your sensitivity to jitter.

Construct an eye diagramRead height, width, jitter and slopePredict how α, ISI and noise change the eyeUse eye diagrams for multi-level signals
⏱ 45 minBTL-3 Apply · BTL-4 Analyse

ConceptHow to read an eye

Construction

Trigger the scope at the symbol rate and display 2 symbol periods. Every possible neighbour pattern traces a different path; with ISI memory of \(L\) symbols there are \(2^{2L+1}\) traces for binary signals.

Multi-level

An M-level PAM signal shows \(M-1\) eyes stacked vertically. Each eye is \(1/(M-1)\) as tall, which is the M-PAM noise penalty seen directly.

DerivationWhat sets the eye’s shape

  1. Height. With ISI, the worst-case opening is \(h_0-\sum_{k\ne0}|h_k|\) (L2). Noise shrinks it further; the probability of error for the worst pattern is \(Q(\text{opening}/\sigma)\). The height reduction in dB, \(20\log_{10}(\text{opening}/h_0)\), is the SNR penalty.

  2. Width and jitter. Zero crossings of RC pulses spread in time when α is small (slow tails). With α = 1 all crossings pass through \(\pm T/2\) exactly: no data-dependent jitter, which is why clock-recovery circuits like large α.

  3. Slope. Near the sampling instant the eye edges have slope \(s\). A timing error \(\tau\) reduces the opening by about \(s\tau\): steep sides (small α) mean high sensitivity.

  4. Best instant. Sample where the eye is tallest; threshold at the eye centre. A timing-recovery loop (Gardner, Mueller–Müller; WiSpec S12) keeps the receiver there automatically.

InteractiveMake your own eye diagram

Raised-cosine BPSK, 300 random symbols. Reduce α and watch the zero crossings spread; narrow the channel and watch the eye close; add noise and watch it fill in.

Worked examplesSolved numericals

Example 1 · Height penalty dB
Given: eye height 0.6 of the ideal.

\(20\log_{10}0.6=-4.4\) dB: the link needs 4.4 dB more SNR than an ISI-free one for the same worst-case error rate.

Answer: 4.4 dB.

Example 2 · Number of traces construction
Given: binary signal, ISI from one symbol on each side.

Patterns of 3 symbols: \(2^3=8\) distinct traces.

Answer: 8.

Example 3 · 4-PAM eye multi-level
Given: 4-level signal, peak-to-peak 2.

3 eyes, each \(2/3\) tall at best (versus 2 for binary): about 9.5 dB less margin at equal peak amplitude.

Answer: 3 eyes of height 2/3.

Example 4 · Timing margin width
Given: zero-crossing jitter ±0.15 T.

Usable width \(1-2\times0.15=0.7T\).

Answer: 0.7 T.

Example 5 · From an E5 run measured
Given: RRC/RRC, α = 0.35, 0.2 T timing error, no noise.

Opening falls from 0.993 to 0.454 (E5); with α = 1 it is still 0.761.

Answer: larger α tolerates timing error better.

Lecture 7 · M3 Pulse Shaping and ISI · CO3

Equalization: undo the channel, or at least most of it

When the channel itself closes the eye, no pulse shape can save you. An equalizer, a short adaptive filter at the receiver, learns the inverse of the channel from a known training sequence and reopens the eye. (Full treatment in WCPS.)

Explain zero-forcing and its noise enhancementExplain MMSE equalizationRun the LMS update by handName where equalizers are used
⏱ 40 minBTL-2 Understand

ConceptThree ideas

Zero-forcing (ZF)

Choose taps so that channel × equalizer ≈ a single delayed impulse. Removes ISI completely but amplifies noise wherever the channel is weak.

MMSE

Minimise \(E|a_{n-D}-y_n|^2\): balances residual ISI against noise. Better than ZF at low SNR.

Adaptive (LMS)

Learn MMSE taps on the fly: \(\mathbf w\leftarrow\mathbf w+\mu e_n\mathbf x_n^*\). Uses a training sequence first, then its own decisions.

Analogy: noise-cancelling headphonesThe headphones learn the sound path to your ear and play the inverse. An equalizer learns the channel’s smearing and applies the inverse before the decision.

DerivationZF, noise enhancement and LMS

  1. Model. Sampled channel \(c=[c_0,c_1,\dots]\); received \(x_n=\sum_kc_ka_{n-k}+w_n\). A linear equalizer with taps \(\mathbf w\) outputs \(y_n=\mathbf w^T\mathbf x_n\).

  2. Zero-forcing. Solve \(\mathbf c\ast\mathbf w=\delta[n-D]\). Example: \(c=[1,0.5]\Rightarrow w=[1,-0.5,0.25,-0.125,\dots]\). With 3 taps the residual ISI is \(0.125\).

  3. Noise enhancement. White noise of variance \(\sigma^2\) leaves the equalizer with variance \(\sigma^2\sum|w_k|^2\). For \(w=[1,-0.5,0.25]\): \(\sum w^2=1.3125\), a 1.2 dB loss. Channels with deep spectral nulls make \(\sum w^2\) huge.

    \[ \sigma_{\text{out}}^2=\sigma^2\sum_k|w_k|^2 \]

  4. LMS. Gradient descent on the squared error with the instantaneous gradient:

    \[ e_n=d_n-y_n,\qquad \mathbf w_{n+1}=\mathbf w_n+\mu\,e_n\,\mathbf x_n^* ,\qquad 0\lt \mu\lt \frac{2}{L\,P_x} \]

    Practice: \(d_n\) is the known training symbol, later the receiver’s own decision. Smaller μ converges slower but with less excess noise.

  5. Decision-feedback equalizer (DFE). Subtract the ISI of already-decided symbols with a feedback filter; avoids noise enhancement from post-cursors. OFDM (Module 4) avoids long time-domain equalizers altogether: one complex multiply per subcarrier.

InteractiveWatch an LMS equalizer learn

BPSK through a 3-tap channel [c₀, 1, c₂], 15-tap LMS equalizer, 2000 training symbols then decision-directed. When |c₀| + |c₂| ≥ 1 the eye is closed before equalization.

Worked examplesSolved numericals

Example 1 · 3-tap ZF residual ISI
Given: channel \([1,\ 0.5]\), equalizer \([1,\ -0.5,\ 0.25]\).

Convolution: \([1,\ 0,\ 0,\ 0.125]\).

Answer: residual ISI 0.125.

Example 2 · Noise enhancement ZF cost
Given: equalizer \([1,\ -0.5,\ 0.25]\).

\(\sum w^2=1.3125\Rightarrow10\log1.3125\).

Answer: 1.18 dB.

Example 3 · LMS step bound stability
Given: 21 taps, input power 2.

\(\mu\lt 2/(21\times2)=0.048\).

Answer: μ < 0.048 (use about one tenth of it).

Example 4 · E6 results ZF vs LMS
Given: channel \([0.45,\ 1,\ 0.65]\), QPSK, SNR 20 dB.

No equalizer: SER 0.375 (eye closed). ZF: 0.034 (noise enhancement 22.8×). LMS/MMSE: 0.016.

Answer: LMS beats ZF by avoiding noise enhancement.

Example 5 · Training overhead GSM
Given: 26-bit training sequence in a 148-bit burst.

\(26/148\).

Answer: 17.6 % of the burst.

A Viterbi equalizer uses the 26-bit midamble to handle up to about 16 µs of multipath.

Long adaptive equalizers (and OFDM in DSL) cope with severe cable ISI.

Common mistakesWatch out

  • Expecting ZF to be best at low SNR: noise enhancement often makes it worse than no equalizer.
  • Choosing μ too large: LMS diverges.
  • Running decision-directed mode before the eye is open: wrong decisions teach wrong taps.

Lecture 8 · Lab · M3 Pulse Shaping and ISI · CO3

Lab: shape the pulses, add noise, watch the eye close

The syllabus lab. Build an RRC transmitter and matched receiver in Python, plot the eye diagram at four noise levels, measure the eye opening and the BER, then repeat with a timing error for several roll-offs.

Design RRC filtersBuild Tx → AWGN → matched filter → samplerPlot eye diagrams at varying SNRMeasure eye opening and BER
⏱ 2 h labBTL-3 Apply

ProcedureAim, equipment and procedure

Aim

Simulate raised-cosine pulse shaping (RRC at transmitter and receiver), display eye diagrams at Eb/N0 = ∞, 20, 10 and 4 dB, and observe eye closure.

You need

Python 3 with numpy and matplotlib (the RRC formula is coded by hand in rcos.py; no toolbox). Optional: GNU Radio 3.10.

  1. Filter: RRC with α = 0.35, 16 samples/symbol, span ±8 symbols (257 taps), normalised to unit energy.

  2. Transmit: place ±1 impulses every 16 samples and convolve with the RRC.

  3. Channel: add Gaussian noise with variance \(N_0/2\) per sample, \(N_0=1/(E_b/N_0)\).

  4. Receive: convolve with the same RRC (matched filter); total delay = 2 × 8 × 16 samples.

  5. Eye: cut the output into 2-symbol segments centred on each sampling instant and overlay them.

  6. Measure: mean and worst-case eye opening, BER; then repeat without noise at τ = 0.2 T for α = 0.1, 0.35, 0.6, 1.

ResultsWhat a correct run gives

Observation table (captured output)

Eb/N0 (dB)  eye height (mean)  eye height (worst)       BER
  no noise              1.000               0.993    0.0000
Eb/N0 = 20 dB              1.000               0.754    0.0000
Eb/N0 = 10 dB              1.004               0.349    0.0000
Eb/N0 = 4 dB              0.993              -0.523    0.0123

alpha  opening at t=0  opening at t=0.2T

What to write in the record

  • The noise-free eye is fully open (worst-case 0.99): RRC ⊗ RRC is zero-ISI.
  • At 4 dB the worst-case opening is negative: the eye is closed and BER ≈ Q(√(2Eb/N0)) = 0.0125, as measured.
  • With a 0.2 T timing error, small α loses most of the eye (0.11 at α = 0.1) while α = 1 keeps 0.76.
Python · e5_eye_lab.py numpy, matplotlib
"""E5  Syllabus lab: raised-cosine pulse shaping and eye diagrams at varying SNR (Module 3, CO3).
Transmit RRC, receive RRC (overall raised cosine), BPSK, alpha = 0.35.
Requires: numpy, matplotlib.   Run: python e5_eye_lab.py"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from rcos import rrc

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
sps, span, alpha, nsym = 16, 8, 0.35, 3000
h = rrc(np.arange(-span*sps, span*sps + 1)/sps, alpha); h /= np.sqrt(np.sum(h**2))
b = rng.integers(0, 2, nsym); x = np.zeros(nsym*sps); x[::sps] = 2*b - 1
tx = np.convolve(x, h)                                  # transmitted baseband signal (Eb = 1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(17, 4))
print(f"{'Eb/N0 (dB)':>10s} {'eye height (mean)':>18s} {'eye height (worst)':>19s} {'BER':>9s}")
for a, EbN0 in zip(ax, [None, 20, 10, 4]):
    if EbN0 is None: r = tx; lab = 'no noise'
    else:
        N0 = 1/10**(EbN0/10); r = tx + rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(N0/2), tx.size); lab = f'Eb/N0 = {EbN0} dB'
    y = np.convolve(r, h)                               # matched filter
    d0 = 2*span*sps                                     # total filter delay
    z = y[d0::sps][:nsym]
    ones, zeros = z[b == 1], z[b == 0]
    hm = (ones.mean() - zeros.mean())/2; hw = (ones.min() - zeros.max())/2
    ber = np.mean((z > 0) != b)
    print(f"{lab:>10s} {hm:18.3f} {hw:19.3f} {ber:9.4f}")
    for i in range(50, 450):
        s0 = d0 + i*sps - sps
        a.plot(np.arange(2*sps + 1)/sps - 1, y[s0:s0 + 2*sps + 1], color='C0', alpha=.12)
    a.axvline(0, color='r', lw=.8); a.set(title=f'{lab}\nworst-case opening {hw:+.2f}', xlabel='t / T', ylim=(-2, 2)); a.grid(alpha=.35)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig('../img/e5_eye.png', dpi=110)

# eye versus roll-off without noise, with a 0.2 T sampling-time error
print(f"\n{'alpha':>5s} {'opening at t=0':>15s} {'opening at t=0.2T':>18s}")
for al in [0.1, 0.35, 0.6, 1.0]:
    g = rrc(np.arange(-span*sps, span*sps + 1)/sps, al); g /= np.sqrt(np.sum(g**2))
    y = np.convolve(np.convolve(x, g), g)
    d0 = 2*span*sps; out = []
    for off in (0, int(0.2*sps)):
        z = y[d0 + off::sps][20:nsym - 20]; bb = b[20:nsym - 20]
        out.append((z[bb == 1].min() - z[bb == 0].max())/2)
    print(f"{al:5.2f} {out[0]:15.3f} {out[1]:18.3f}")
Python · rcos.py helper: RC and RRC formulas
"""Shared helper: raised-cosine and root-raised-cosine impulse responses (unit peak / unit energy)."""
import numpy as np

def rc(t, alpha, T=1.0):
    """Raised cosine p(t) with p(0) = 1 and zeros at t = nT."""
    t = np.asarray(t, float); x = t/T
    with np.errstate(divide='ignore', invalid='ignore'):
        p = np.sinc(x)*np.cos(np.pi*alpha*x)/(1 - (2*alpha*x)**2)
    if alpha > 0:
        sing = np.isclose(np.abs(2*alpha*x), 1.0)
        p[sing] = np.pi/4*np.sinc(1/(2*alpha))
    return p

def rrc(t, alpha, T=1.0):
    """Root raised cosine with unit energy over symbol period T."""
    t = np.asarray(t, float); x = t/T; h = np.zeros_like(x)
    a = alpha
    z = np.isclose(x, 0)
    h[z] = 1 - a + 4*a/np.pi
    if a > 0:
        s = np.isclose(np.abs(x), 1/(4*a))
        h[s] = a/np.sqrt(2)*((1 + 2/np.pi)*np.sin(np.pi/(4*a)) + (1 - 2/np.pi)*np.cos(np.pi/(4*a)))
    else:
        s = np.zeros_like(z)
    o = ~(z | s)
    xo = x[o]
    h[o] = (np.sin(np.pi*xo*(1 - a)) + 4*a*xo*np.cos(np.pi*xo*(1 + a)))/(np.pi*xo*(1 - (4*a*xo)**2))
    return h/np.sqrt(T)

  2. Why is the total delay 2 × span × sps samples?

"""E1  Why shape pulses: time shape and spectrum of rectangular, sinc and raised-cosine pulses (Module 3, CO3).
Requires: numpy, matplotlib.   Run: python e1_pulse_spectra.py"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from rcos import rc

T, sps = 1.0, 32                         # symbol period and samples per symbol
t = np.arange(-16*sps, 16*sps + 1)/sps
pulses = {'rectangular (NRZ)': (np.abs(t) < 0.5).astype(float),
          'sinc (α = 0)': rc(t, 0.0),
          'raised cosine α = 0.25': rc(t, 0.25),
          'raised cosine α = 0.5': rc(t, 0.5),
          'raised cosine α = 1': rc(t, 1.0)}
N = 2**15
f = np.fft.fftshift(np.fft.fftfreq(N, 1/sps))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.6))
print(f"{'pulse':>24s} {'99% power BW (×Rs)':>19s} {'level at f = 1.5 Rs (dB)':>25s}")
for name, p in pulses.items():
    P = np.abs(np.fft.fftshift(np.fft.fft(p, N)))**2; P /= P.max()
    pos = f >= 0; cum = np.cumsum(P[pos]); cum /= cum[-1]
    b99 = f[pos][np.argmax(cum >= 0.99)]
    lvl = 10*np.log10(P[np.argmin(abs(f - 1.5))] + 1e-12)
    print(f"{name:>24s} {b99:19.3f} {lvl:25.1f}")
    ax[0].plot(t, p, label=name); ax[1].plot(f, 10*np.log10(P + 1e-12), label=name)
ax[0].set(xlim=(-5, 5), xlabel='t / T', title='Pulse shapes: RC and sinc cross zero at every other symbol instant')
ax[1].set(xlim=(0, 3), ylim=(-80, 3), xlabel='f / Rs', ylabel='dB', title='Power spectrum: RC is confined to (1 + α) Rs / 2')
for a in ax: a.grid(alpha=.35); a.legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig('../img/e1_pulses.png', dpi=110)

"""E2  ISI: a random NRZ sequence through a first-order RC channel of bandwidth B (Module 3, CO3).
Requires: numpy, scipy, matplotlib.   Run: python e2_isi_channel.py"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.signal import lfilter

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
sps = 64; nsym = 400
a = 2*rng.integers(0, 2, nsym) - 1
x = np.repeat(a, sps).astype(float)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(15, 6.5))
print(f"{'B/Rb':>5s} {'worst-case eye opening':>23s} {'peak distortion D':>18s}")
for k, BRb in enumerate([2.0, 0.5, 0.25]):
    fc = BRb/sps                                  # cut-off in cycles per sample (Rb = 1/sps)
    al = np.exp(-2*np.pi*fc)                      # one-pole RC low-pass (impulse invariant)
    y = lfilter([1 - al], [1, -al], x)
    # single-pulse response sampled at the end of each symbol: main cursor and tails
    h = lfilter([1 - al], [1, -al], np.r_[np.ones(sps), np.zeros(10*sps)])
    cur = h[sps - 1::sps][:11]                     # samples at t = (n+1)T - one sample
    D = np.sum(np.abs(cur[1:]))/cur[0]
    samp = y[sps - 1::sps][20:]
    eye = (samp[a[20:] > 0].min() - samp[a[20:] < 0].max())/2
    print(f"{BRb:5.2f} {eye:23.3f} {D:18.3f}")
    n = 16*sps
    ax[0, k].plot(np.arange(n)/sps, x[:n], 'k--', lw=.8); ax[0, k].plot(np.arange(n)/sps, y[:n])
    ax[0, k].set(title=f'B = {BRb} Rb', xlabel='t / Tb')
    for i in range(30, 200):
        seg = y[i*sps - sps//2:i*sps + 3*sps//2]
        ax[1, k].plot(np.arange(len(seg))/sps, seg, color='C0', alpha=.15)
    ax[1, k].set(title=f'eye diagram: opening {max(eye, 0):.2f}', xlabel='t / Tb')
for a_ in ax.flat: a_.grid(alpha=.35)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig('../img/e2_isi.png', dpi=110)

Python · e3_nyquist_rc_design.py numpy
"""E3  Nyquist's first criterion: RC pulses have zero ISI; folded spectrum is flat; RRC ⊗ RRC = RC (Module 3, CO3).
Requires: numpy, matplotlib.   Run: python e3_nyquist_rc_design.py"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from rcos import rc, rrc

sps, span = 8, 8                                 # samples/symbol, filter span in symbols each side
n = np.arange(-span*sps, span*sps + 1)
print(f"{'alpha':>5s} {'max |p(kT)|, k≠0':>17s} {'folded-spectrum ripple (dB)':>28s} {'RRC*RRC vs RC error':>20s} {'taps':>5s}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4.4))
for alpha in [0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0]:
    p = rc(n/sps, alpha)
    isi = np.max(np.abs(p[::sps][np.arange(len(p[::sps])) != span]))
    N = 4096; P = np.abs(np.fft.fft(p, N))/sps           # P(f)/T; f in units of Rs*sps/N
    f = np.fft.fftfreq(N, 1/sps)
    fold = sum(np.interp((np.linspace(-.5, .5, 201) + k), np.fft.fftshift(f), np.fft.fftshift(P)) for k in range(-3, 4))
    rip = 20*np.log10(fold.max()/fold.min())
    h = rrc(n/sps, alpha)/np.sqrt(sps)
    g = np.convolve(h, h); g = g[len(h)//2:len(h)//2 + len(p)]
    err = np.max(np.abs(g/g.max() - p)) if alpha > 0 else np.nan
    print(f"{alpha:5.2f} {isi:17.2e} {rip:28.3f} {err:20.4f} {len(n):5d}")
    ax[0].plot(n/sps, p, label=f'α = {alpha}')
    ax[1].plot(np.fft.fftshift(f), np.fft.fftshift(P), label=f'α = {alpha}')
    if alpha in (0.25, 0.5):
        ax[2].plot(np.linspace(-.5, .5, 201), fold, label=f'Σ P(f − k Rs), α = {alpha}')
ax[0].plot(np.arange(-span, span + 1), np.zeros(2*span + 1), 'k.', ms=8)
ax[0].set(xlim=(-6, 6), title='Zero crossings at every t = kT (dots)', xlabel='t / T')
ax[1].set(xlim=(-1.2, 1.2), title='Spectrum P(f)/T: bandwidth (1 + α) Rs / 2', xlabel='f / Rs')
ax[2].set(ylim=(0.9, 1.1), title='Folded spectrum is flat: Nyquist criterion', xlabel='f / Rs')
for a in ax: a.grid(alpha=.35); a.legend(fontsize=8)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig('../img/e3_nyquist.png', dpi=110)

Python · e4_matched_filter.py numpy, scipy
"""E4  Matched filter: output SNR of matched vs mismatched receive filters, and BER of RRC-matched BPSK (Module 3, CO3).
Requires: numpy, scipy, matplotlib.   Run: python e4_matched_filter.py"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.special import erfc
from scipy.signal import lfilter
from rcos import rrc

Q = lambda x: 0.5*erfc(x/np.sqrt(2))
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)
sps = 16
p = np.ones(sps)/np.sqrt(sps)                     # unit-energy rectangular pulse
N0 = 0.1
print("Rectangular pulse, E = 1, N0 = 0.1  -> theory 2E/N0 = 20 (13.01 dB)")
print(f"{'receive filter':>30s} {'peak SNR (dB)':>14s} {'loss vs matched (dB)':>21s}")
def snr_of(h):
    y = np.convolve(p, h); k = np.argmax(np.abs(y))
    return y[k]**2/(N0/2*np.sum(h**2))
ref = snr_of(p[::-1])
for name, h in [('matched (rectangular)', p[::-1]),
                ('RC low-pass, B = 0.5 Rs', None), ('RC low-pass, B = 1 Rs', None), ('RC low-pass, B = 2 Rs', None),
                ('integrate over half a symbol', np.ones(sps//2))]:
    if h is None:
        B = float(name.split('= ')[1].split(' ')[0]); al = np.exp(-2*np.pi*B/sps)
        h = lfilter([1 - al], [1, -al], np.r_[1, np.zeros(20*sps)])
    s = snr_of(h)
    print(f"{name:>30s} {10*np.log10(s):14.2f} {10*np.log10(ref/s):21.2f}")

# BPSK with RRC transmit + RRC matched receive (alpha 0.35), Monte-Carlo BER
a, span = 0.35, 8
h = rrc(np.arange(-span*sps, span*sps + 1)/sps, a); h /= np.sqrt(np.sum(h**2))
print(f"\nBPSK, RRC α = {a} Tx and matched Rx, {span*2+1}-symbol filters")
print(f"{'Eb/N0':>6s} {'BER sim':>10s} {'theory':>10s}")
E_ = []; S_ = []
for d in range(0, 10, 2):
    nb = 200_000; b = rng.integers(0, 2, nb); x = np.zeros(nb*sps); x[::sps] = 2*b - 1
    s = np.convolve(x, h)
    N0 = 1/10**(d/10)
    r = s + rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(N0/2), s.size)
    z = np.convolve(r, h)[2*span*sps::sps][:nb]
    ber = np.mean((z > 0) != b); E_.append(d); S_.append(ber)
    print(f"{d:6d} {ber:10.2e} {Q(np.sqrt(2*10**(d/10))):10.2e}")
xx = np.linspace(0, 9, 100)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4.4))
t = np.arange(-span*sps, span*sps + 1)/sps
ax[0].plot(t, h/h.max(), label='RRC (transmit = receive)'); g = np.convolve(h, h); ax[0].plot(np.arange(len(g))/sps - 2*span, g/g.max(), label='RRC ⊗ RRC = RC')
ax[0].set(xlim=(-5, 5), xlabel='t / T', title='Matched pair: each filter alone has ISI, the cascade has none'); ax[0].legend()
ax[1].semilogy(xx, Q(np.sqrt(2*10**(xx/10))), 'k', label='Q(√(2Eb/N0))'); ax[1].semilogy(E_, S_, 'o', mfc='none', label='RRC-matched BPSK, simulated')
ax[1].set(xlabel='Eb/N0 (dB)', ylabel='BER', title='Matched filtering reaches the BPSK bound'); ax[1].legend()
for a_ in ax: a_.grid(alpha=.35, which='both')
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig('../img/e4_matched.png', dpi=110)

"""E5  Syllabus lab: raised-cosine pulse shaping and eye diagrams at varying SNR (Module 3, CO3).
Transmit RRC, receive RRC (overall raised cosine), BPSK, alpha = 0.35.
Requires: numpy, matplotlib.   Run: python e5_eye_lab.py"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from rcos import rrc

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
sps, span, alpha, nsym = 16, 8, 0.35, 3000
h = rrc(np.arange(-span*sps, span*sps + 1)/sps, alpha); h /= np.sqrt(np.sum(h**2))
b = rng.integers(0, 2, nsym); x = np.zeros(nsym*sps); x[::sps] = 2*b - 1
tx = np.convolve(x, h)                                  # transmitted baseband signal (Eb = 1)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(17, 4))
print(f"{'Eb/N0 (dB)':>10s} {'eye height (mean)':>18s} {'eye height (worst)':>19s} {'BER':>9s}")
for a, EbN0 in zip(ax, [None, 20, 10, 4]):
    if EbN0 is None: r = tx; lab = 'no noise'
    else:
        N0 = 1/10**(EbN0/10); r = tx + rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(N0/2), tx.size); lab = f'Eb/N0 = {EbN0} dB'
    y = np.convolve(r, h)                               # matched filter
    d0 = 2*span*sps                                     # total filter delay
    z = y[d0::sps][:nsym]
    ones, zeros = z[b == 1], z[b == 0]
    hm = (ones.mean() - zeros.mean())/2; hw = (ones.min() - zeros.max())/2
    ber = np.mean((z > 0) != b)
    print(f"{lab:>10s} {hm:18.3f} {hw:19.3f} {ber:9.4f}")
    for i in range(50, 450):
        s0 = d0 + i*sps - sps
        a.plot(np.arange(2*sps + 1)/sps - 1, y[s0:s0 + 2*sps + 1], color='C0', alpha=.12)
    a.axvline(0, color='r', lw=.8); a.set(title=f'{lab}\nworst-case opening {hw:+.2f}', xlabel='t / T', ylim=(-2, 2)); a.grid(alpha=.35)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig('../img/e5_eye.png', dpi=110)

Python · e6_lms_equalizer.py numpy
"""E6  Adaptive LMS equalizer for a 3-tap ISI channel, compared with zero-forcing (Module 3, CO3).
Requires: numpy, matplotlib.   Run: python e6_lms_equalizer.py"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(6)
c = np.array([0.45, 1.0, 0.65])              # channel: pre-cursor, main, post-cursor
N, L, mu, delay = 12000, 21, 0.004, 11        # symbols, equalizer taps, step size, decision delay
snr_db = 20
a = (2*rng.integers(0, 2, N) - 1) + 1j*(2*rng.integers(0, 2, N) - 1)   # QPSK symbols (Es = 2)
r = np.convolve(a, c)[:N]
r += np.sqrt(2*10**(-snr_db/10)/2)*(rng.normal(size=N) + 1j*rng.normal(size=N))
w = np.zeros(L, complex); w[L//2] = 1
mse = []; out = np.zeros(N, complex)
for n in range(L, N):
    u = r[n - L + 1:n + 1][::-1]
    y = np.dot(w, u); out[n] = y
    d = a[n - delay] if n < 4000 else (np.sign(y.real) + 1j*np.sign(y.imag))  # training then decision-directed
    e = d - y
    w += mu*e*np.conj(u)
    mse.append(abs(e)**2)
# zero-forcing (least-squares inverse of the channel, same length)
C = np.zeros((L + 2, L)); [C.__setitem__((slice(i, i + 3), i), c) for i in range(L)]
target = np.zeros(L + 2); target[delay] = 1
wzf = np.linalg.lstsq(C, target, rcond=None)[0]
def ser(z, dly):
    det = np.sign(z.real) + 1j*np.sign(z.imag)
    return np.mean(det[8000:] != a[8000 - dly:N - dly])
print(f"Channel taps {c};  noise enhancement of ZF = {np.sum(np.abs(wzf)**2):.2f} (×), MMSE/LMS avoids most of it")
print(f"{'receiver':>22s} {'symbol error rate':>18s}")
print(f"{'no equalizer':>22s} {ser(r, 1):18.4f}")
zz = np.convolve(r, wzf)[:N]
print(f"{'zero-forcing':>22s} {ser(zz, delay):18.4f}")
print(f"{'LMS (after training)':>22s} {ser(out, delay):18.4f}")
print(f"Final MSE (last 1000 symbols): {np.mean(mse[-1000:]):.4f}")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4.4))
ax[0].plot(r[8000:].real, r[8000:].imag, '.', ms=2); ax[0].set(title='Before equalizer (ISI)', aspect='equal')
ax[1].plot(out[8000:].real, out[8000:].imag, '.', ms=2); ax[1].set(title='After LMS equalizer', aspect='equal')
ax[2].semilogy(np.convolve(mse, np.ones(50)/50, 'valid')); ax[2].set(title='LMS learning curve (MSE)', xlabel='symbol')
for a_ in ax: a_.grid(alpha=.35)
fig.tight_layout(); fig.savefig('../img/e6_lms.png', dpi=110)

"""E7  Sensitivity to sampling-time error: BER of RC-shaped BPSK versus timing offset and roll-off (Module 3, CO3).
Requires: numpy, scipy, matplotlib.   Run: python e7_timing_jitter.py"""
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from rcos import rc

rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
EbN0 = 8; N0 = 1/10**(EbN0/10)
nsym = 200_000; span = 12
b = rng.integers(0, 2, nsym); a = 2*b - 1
offs = np.linspace(0, 0.4, 9)
print(f"Eb/N0 = {EbN0} dB; overall pulse = raised cosine; noise after matched filter has variance N0/2")
print(f"{'tau/T':>6s} " + ' '.join(f'{"α="+str(al):>9s}' for al in [0.1, 0.35, 0.6, 1.0]))
res = {}
for al in [0.1, 0.35, 0.6, 1.0]:
    B = []
    for tau in offs:
        k = np.arange(-span, span + 1); g = rc(k + tau, al)        # samples of the overall pulse at kT + tau
        z = np.convolve(a, g)[span:span + nsym] + rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(N0/2), nsym)
        B.append(np.mean((z > 0) != b))
    res[al] = B
for i, tau in enumerate(offs):
    print(f"{tau:6.2f} " + ' '.join(f'{res[al][i]:9.2e}' for al in res))
plt.figure(figsize=(7.5, 4.8))
for al, B in res.items(): plt.semilogy(offs, np.maximum(B, 1e-6), 'o-', label=f'α = {al}')
plt.xlabel('sampling-time error τ / T'); plt.ylabel('BER'); plt.grid(alpha=.35, which='both'); plt.legend()
plt.title('Larger roll-off: more bandwidth, more timing tolerance'); plt.tight_layout(); plt.savefig('../img/e7_timing.png', dpi=110)

Quick check15 questions (20 minutes)

1. The power spectrum of a random pulse train is proportional to U · Easy

Rs/2.

(1 + α)Rs.

4. Nyquist’s first criterion in frequency states that R · Easy

Folded spectrum flat.

sinc × 1/t².

6. With RRC filters at Tx and Rx, the overall response is U · Easy

√P × √P.

7. The matched filter for p(t) has impulse response R · Easy

8. Maximum matched-filter output SNR is R · Easy

Cauchy–Schwarz bound.

9. In an eye diagram, the vertical opening indicates U · Easy

Eye height.

10. Sampled pulse [0.2, 1, 0.3, 0.1]. Peak distortion D is Ap · Easy

0.2 + 0.3 + 0.1.

1 − 2e^(−π/2) = 0.584.

They invert weak parts of the channel.

Stochastic gradient.

14. Larger roll-off α gives An · Medium

Trade-off.

M − 1.

DescriptiveA1–A8

A1. Explain why rectangular pulses are unsuitable for band-limited radio channels. Sketch their spectrum.

Solution faculty
sinc² spectrum, −13.3 dB first sidelobe, 1/f² decay; adjacent-channel interference (L1).

A2. What is ISI? Derive the worst-case eye opening of NRZ through a first-order RC channel.

Solution faculty
Main cursor 1 − x, tails (1 − x)xⁿ, sum x, opening 1 − 2x, x = e^(−T/τ) (L2).

A3. State and prove Nyquist’s first criterion. Show that the minimum bandwidth is Rs/2.

Solution faculty
Sampling ↔ periodic spectrum; p(nT) = δ[n] ⇔ ΣP(f − k/T) = T; gaps if W < 1/2T (L3).

A4. Write the raised-cosine pulse in time and frequency. Explain the role of α and the RRC split.

Solution faculty
Formulas, bandwidth (1 + α)Rs/2, 1/t³ tails, RRC Tx/Rx gives RC + matched filter (L4).

A5. Derive the matched filter using the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and show it equals a correlator.

Solution faculty
L5 derivation; SNRmax = 2E/N0.

A6. Draw and label an eye diagram. How do noise, ISI, roll-off and timing error affect it?

Solution faculty
Height, width, slope, jitter (L6).

A7. Explain ZF, MMSE and LMS equalizers. Why can ZF be worse than no equalizer?

Solution faculty
Noise enhancement Σw² (L7).

A8. Describe the procedure of the eye-diagram lab and the expected observations.

Solution faculty
L8 procedure and results.

NumericalN1–N12

N1. Find the passband bandwidth of a 16-QAM signal at 40 Mb/s with α = 0.25.

Solution faculty
Rs = 10 Mbaud; B = 12.5 MHz.

N2. A 3 kHz baseband channel. Find the maximum zero-ISI symbol rate for α = 0 and α = 0.5.

Solution faculty
6000 and 4000 baud.

N3. An RC channel has τ = 5 µs. Find the worst-case opening at 100 kb/s and 200 kb/s.

Solution faculty
Tb = 10 µs: x = e^(−2) = 0.135 → 0.729. Tb = 5 µs: x = e^(−1) = 0.368 → 0.264.

N4. Sampled pulse [0.1, 0.25, 1, 0.3, 0.15]. Find D and the worst-case opening. Is the eye open?

Solution faculty
D = 0.8; opening 0.2; open.

N5. Compute p(t) of an RC pulse with α = 0.5 at t = 0.5T and t = 1.5T.

Solution faculty
p(0.5T) = 0.637 × cos(π/4)/(1 − 0.25) = 0.600; p(1.5T) = −0.212 × cos(0.75π)/(1 − 2.25) = −0.120.

N6. Rectangular pulse 2 V for 0.5 µs (1 Ω); N0 = 4 × 10⁻⁹ W/Hz. Find matched-filter output SNR and BPSK BER.

Solution faculty
E = 4 × 0.5 × 10⁻⁶ = 2 × 10⁻⁶ J; 2E/N0 = 1000 (30 dB); BER ≈ Q(31.6) ≈ 0.

N7. Find the SNR loss of integrating over 0.7T instead of T for a rectangular pulse.

Solution faculty
Signal 0.7, noise 0.7: SNR ratio 0.7 → 1.55 dB.

N8. Eye height is 0.45 of ideal. Find the SNR penalty and the BER for σ = 0.15 (normalised).

Solution faculty
−6.9 dB; Q(0.45/0.15) = Q(3) = 1.35 × 10⁻³.

N9. Design an RRC FIR: Rs = 250 kbaud, fs = 2 MS/s, span ±6 symbols. How many taps?

Solution faculty
sps = 8; 2 × 6 × 8 + 1 = 97 taps.

N10. Channel [1, 0.4]. Find a 3-tap ZF equalizer, residual ISI and noise enhancement.

Solution faculty
w = [1, −0.4, 0.16]; residual 0.064; Σw² = 1.186 → 0.74 dB.

N11. LMS with 11 taps, input power 1.5. Find the stability bound for μ.

Solution faculty
μ < 2/(11 × 1.5) = 0.121.

N12. DVB-S2 at 30 Mbaud with α = 0.2, 0.25, 0.35. Find each bandwidth.

Solution faculty
36, 37.5, 40.5 MHz.

Lab tasksT1–T4

  1. T1 · Extend E5 to QPSK; plot I and Q eyes and the constellation at the sampling instant.
  2. T2 · Add a two-ray channel h = [1, 0, 0.5] at symbol spacing to E5 and equalize it with LMS (E6).
  3. T3 · In GNU Radio, build RRC Tx → Channel Model → RRC Rx → Symbol Sync (Gardner) and show the recovered constellation.
  4. T4 · MATLAB/Octave: write rrc_taps(alpha, sps, span) and verify RRC ⊗ RRC zero crossings.

RequisitesBefore and after this module

Builds on

SGPS (convolution, Fourier transform, sampling, FIR filters), MFCS (Cauchy–Schwarz, Gaussian noise), M2 (BPSK, correlator, BER).

Leads to

M4 (OFDM removes ISI with a cyclic prefix), M5 (coding on top of an ISI-free link), WCPS (MLSE, DFE, timing and carrier synchronisation in depth).

VerificationWhat was checked, and what was not

  • Programs E1–E7 were run in Python 3.13 (numpy 2.5, scipy 1.18); the outputs and plots on this page are from those runs.
  • The worst-case-opening formula 1 − 2e^(−2πB/Rb) was checked against the E2 simulation (0.914 and 0.584).
  • Worked examples and practice answers were recomputed numerically.
  • Widgets run in the browser; the L8 eye widget uses smoothed noise for display, while its histogram and BER use exact sample-level noise.
  • Standards figures (UMTS and DVB-S2 roll-offs, GSM training length) are well-established values; check current standard texts before examinations.
